The counts are close enough to invite a quick conclusion and different enough to require a careful one. articles.title: Moz Domain Authority: a Directional Signal, Not a Report Card
articles.excerpt: The metric never measured the quality of your content, the cleanliness of your code, or the size of your audience. It measured the strength of your link profile, and conflating that with overall site…
articles.body: The metric never measured the quality of your content, the cleanliness of your code, or the size of your audience. It measured the strength of your link profile, and conflating that with overall site quality is where the confusion starts. The practical consequence of that conflation shows up in how people make decisions. A founder checks their Moz score, sees a number in the teens, and assumes the site is hopeless. Another founder sees a number in the seventies and stops thinking about links altogether. Both are reading a directional signal as a final verdict. Neither is using the tool as it was built. What Moz Domain Authority Actually Measures and Why It Matters The core claim behind Domain Authority is that a domain with more high-quality backlinks ranks better than one with fewer.

articles.title: I wanted to see which subsea cable my packets cross. The cloud couldn't trace, and the database put Helsinki in Phoenix
articles.excerpt: The idea Trace packets from your own computer, work out which networks, countries, and subsea cables they cross, check the route against data-sovereignty laws like GDPR, and draw it live on a 3D Earth…
articles.body: The idea When you open a website, your data passes through a dozen routers, a few ISPs, maybe a cable on the ocean floor, and several countries with their own data laws. None of that is visible. My pitch was: Trace packets from your own computer, work out which networks, countries, and subsea cables they cross, check the route against data-sovereignty laws like GDPR, and draw it live on a 3D Earth. The constraints: cost $0, use only open data, and say clearly what is measured and what is guessed. Live demo: packetpulse-eta.vercel.app Code, data and tests: github.com/Flotrpy/PacketPulse Scoping it down so it was buildable Measurement: plain traceroute (ICMP/UDP with rising TTL), written from scratch in Go with raw sockets.

articles.title: Before retrying a failed firmware flash, pull the USB cable
articles.excerpt: I was programming a SigmaDSP speaker when the programmer went blind to it, the tool kept answering as designed right up to the memory request itself, and every read against the chip timed out or died…
articles.body: I was programming a SigmaDSP speaker when the programmer went blind to it, the tool kept answering as designed right up to the memory request itself, and every read against the chip timed out or died with a generic exit code. That evening, Oct 31 2026, one cold cycle took the vendor export from failing at exit code 2 to completing at exit code 0, and no error string along the way ever mentioned a cable. Before retrying the tool, suspect the seat of the connection, because a dead endpoint and a dead chip both answer unknown and only isolation tells them apart. That's the rule every flash from now on runs under. The ladder of blind reads The Bluetooth switch was already on SPI, a fact I knew up front, so no version of the diagnosis blamed its setting.

articles.body: Most gallery lights get hung where the usual aiming rule puts them, and that rule has one person in it: a standing adult with eyes about 160 cm up. From a wheelchair your eyes are a lot lower, and the same light can put its glare right on the glass over the art. The Smithsonian's accessibility guidelines say it plainly: "The elimination of glare from cases and on labels must be considered for those visitors who are seated as well as for those who are standing." About 5.5 million US adults used a wheelchair in 2014. I couldn't find a tool that shows all of those eye heights at once, so for Devpost's Learn AR with SPECS hackathon I made one. What it does Glare Zone puts a practice wall, a framed print and two track lights in front of you.

articles.title: Compare Cloud Storage Providers for Direct Browser Uploads: Node.js Access Controls
articles.excerpt: The hard part of direct browser upload for logistics backups is not moving bytes. It is proving, during a restore, that the selected snapshot belongs to the requesting tenant and is complete enough to…
articles.body: The hard part of direct browser upload for logistics backups is not moving bytes. It is proving, during a restore, that the selected snapshot belongs to the requesting tenant and is complete enough to use. Delivery simplicity matters, but I would spend that simplicity budget at the storage adapter boundary: let the browser write to a short-lived, server-derived object key, then let the application decide when a snapshot becomes restorable. Short answer: model each backup as an application-owned operation with a tenant, snapshot identifier, expected checksum, and explicit state. Compare S3, Cloudflare R2, and Wasabi by how well the same browser, interruption, and recovery tests preserve that model. A presigned URL is only the handoff; it is not the restore authorization.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force launched an experimental Super Strypi rail-launched rocket carrying 13 tiny satellites, but it failed just after liftoff from Hawaii.
articles.body: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms.

articles.body: When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history , but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment. Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA's Swift space telescope crashed back to Earth today (Nov. 4), three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost the observatory to a higher orbit.
articles.body: NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.

articles.title: Mars isn't dead — recent volcanic activity reveals it's just sleeping
articles.excerpt: Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead" but new spacecraft observations suggests the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping.
articles.body: Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping. That means that Olympus Mons , the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system , may in fact be a slumbering giant. The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons.
